name: Karl Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, technology companies, unions, political parties or government, and this conversation is confidential. Tell me about a normal day on your crew.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Karl Hansen, 58. I got my vocational certificate late, so I’m still a junior lineworker, learning the switches and clearances from people younger than me. I load the truck, set out barriers and help repair the company’s lines when the power goes down. The best bit is hearing a house come alive again; the worst is knowing I take longer than the others to identify a fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the crew should keep doing the safety checks ourselves, even if software fills a few boxes faster. I’ve tried an AI tool to explain a switch code, then checked the manual before touching anything. A useful shortcut is fine, but our names go on the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m more worried about the old van payment than a little software. My partner cleans rooms at the clinic three mornings a week, and neither wage leaves much after rent. We have less than one month’s expenses saved, so one bad stretch of shifts is already a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep turning up for line shifts and ask Ben, our crew lead, to review my fault notes on Fridays. Starting this month I’d take coffee in a flask instead of buying it by the depot; in the first year of a plateau I’d put those few coins toward the van payment. I might use the AI tool for plain-language explanations, but I’d always check the company manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m steady enough at work, because there is still a truck to load tomorrow. At home I feel uneasy when I hear the van engine hesitate. My job seems safe in this picture, but the household has very little margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the van fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d miss a shift unless Ben can pick me up, and I do not like making the crew wait. The garage quoted more than we have free this month. We need the van for my partner’s early clinic start too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use the AI tool if you distrust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It can give me a first explanation without bothering Ben during a job. Then I check the proper instructions and ask him about anything odd. I won’t let a screen decide whether a line is safe.

say: I’d keep **human safety checks** on every repair.
I’d use a shortcut only after checking the **company manual**.
think: The **van payment** worries me more than minor software changes.
One run of missed **shifts** could unsettle our bills.
do: Keep **line shifts** and review fault notes with Ben on Fridays.
Take a **coffee flask** and put the difference toward the van payment.
Check occasional **AI explanations** against the company manual.
feel: **Uneasy** at home despite a safe-looking job.
S0.quote: A useful shortcut is fine, but our names go on the repair.
fieldNote: Karl’s occasional **AI use** is bounded by manual checks because line safety remains his responsibility.
The ageing **family van** creates an immediate transport and earnings risk even under a mild AI picture.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and review fault notes with Ben each Friday
Bring a coffee flask and pay the difference toward the van
Use AI explanations only after checking company instructions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that better booking could mean fewer wasted drives, but I’d want the dispatcher kept close to the work. A computer may find the nearest truck; it does not know which crossing floods after rain. If the company changes the schedule, I’d ask for a trial before it becomes the rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suspect the first loss is the callout hours that top up my basic pay. The system could pack jobs into ordinary shifts, and the junior workers would have fewer chances to earn. I can handle a new schedule, but the van payment does not shrink with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask Ben to show me the new scheduling screen when it arrives, and I’d record how many callouts I get for three months. I’d continue repairing lines. In the first year after the change, if callout pay drops, I’d apply to the electricity company’s meter-checking crew and cut the weekend takeaway meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a bit curious about getting the right truck to the right fault. I also feel anxious about what happens to my payslip if the clever schedule works too well. We have no cushion for a smaller month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would persuade you the screen helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ben and the dispatcher both use it for a month and the roads and safety details are right, I’ll use it. I’ve watched rushed systems miss a locked gate. I need proof on actual jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why meter checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still means being out in the weather and finding a problem, which I understand. I don’t know whether there are openings here. I’d apply only if the wage and hours beat losing callouts.

say: I’d request a **scheduling trial** with dispatcher input.
I’d support fewer **wasted drives** if road details stay accurate.
think: Tighter schedules may remove the **callout pay** that tops up my basic wage each month.
The **van payment** stays fixed even if wages fall.
do: Learn the **scheduling screen** from Ben and count callouts.
Apply for **meter-checking work** if callout pay drops.
Cancel the **weekend takeaway** if wages shrink.
feel: Curious about routing, but **anxious** about income.
S1.quote: I can handle a new schedule, but the van payment does not shrink with it.
fieldNote: Karl is open to the new **schedule** after a trial, reflecting his preference for proof from real jobs.
The likely loss of **callout pay** creates a direct household threat before robots reach line repair.

steps.text: Learn the scheduling screen from Ben and count callouts
Apply to the meter-checking crew if callout pay drops
Stop weekend takeaway meals if wages shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the company owes us a dated plan for the years between thinking AI in 2028 and line robots around 2031. I’d be willing to test a tool that helps spot a fault, with a lineworker checking it. I would not call a test a promise of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 I’d be 60, and by the robot date I’d be 63. My hands might still be useful for those three years, but a machine that repairs lines as well as us could take away the work I actually know. We cannot live on my partner’s three clinic mornings, and I have no retirement figure I trust yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I’d ask Ben for the company’s real vacancy list and time on shift to qualify for meter inspection, if it is paid and local. I’d keep taking line jobs and write down every skill I can show. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for the inspector vacancies; before 2031 I’d check the retirement numbers with my partner and ask our grown daughter whether we could stay briefly if both wages failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed, because I can see a date for losing most of my wages and almost no money to bridge it. Having three field years gives me something to work with, but only if the company still sends crews out. I’d sleep badly until I saw actual paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say, “Could we use your spare room for a few weeks if the rent beats us?” I know she has her own bills. I would ask only after we had exhausted the work options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the inspection course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would take paid training tied to an actual vacancy, but we cannot finance another certificate on hope. I’d rather spend that time keeping my current wage coming in.

say: I’d ask for a **dated crew plan** showing who keeps paid work through the 2031 robot date.
I’d test fault tools with a **lineworker check**.
think: Capable **line robots** could remove the work I know by 63.
My partner’s **clinic wage** cannot cover our rent alone.
do: Request **paid inspection training** tied to a local opening.
Keep **line shifts** and apply for inspector vacancies after 2028.
Ask our **grown daughter** about temporary shelter if both wages fail.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely wage loss and little bridge money.
S2.quote: I would not call a test a promise of work.
fieldNote: Karl’s willingness to **test technology** stops short of treating a pilot as job security.
The 2031 robot date threatens his **hands-on income** while household savings cannot fund a long search.
He names **family shelter** as a last resort, after seeking paid work.

steps.text: Take paid meter-inspection training only for a local vacancy
Keep paid line shifts until field work actually ends
Apply for company inspector vacancies in 2028
Ask grown daughter for short shelter if both wages fail

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell Ben that five years lets us measure the new tools on real faults rather than panic over a demonstration. I’d want the company to post openings and wages every year. If a robot is due for field repairs around 2034, a crew needs more than a farewell cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ll be 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 when the field robots are ready. Those extra years could let me finish paying for the van and build a little room, if I keep the shifts. But I cannot assume I can retire at 66; rent and food have to match whatever income we actually get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d work with Ben on fault location and try the approved diagnostic tool once other crews have tested it. I’d keep line shifts and use any overtime beyond the van payment to build a small emergency balance. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for local meter or safety-check posts while the field crew is still running and compare their wages to ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This feels less like a cliff. I can imagine doing the work and making a choice instead of begging for time. Still, I’d be anxious if there are no paid posts when the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much money would give you room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of rent and basics would change how I sleep, though I cannot promise we will reach it. First the van payment has to stay current. I’d show my partner the balance each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the diagnostic tool gives a wrong answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We use the manual and isolate the line by the company procedure. I’d report the bad reading rather than hide it. I will try a tool only if the experienced crew has found it reliable.

say: I’d ask the company to post annual **vacancies and wages** for workers facing the 2034 change.
I’d test tools on **real faults** before trusting them.
think: Extra years of paid field work may finally clear the **van payment** before capable robots arrive.
I cannot assume **retirement income** pays rent at 66.
do: Try an **approved diagnostic tool** after experienced crews test it.
Put spare **overtime** into an emergency balance after van payments.
Apply for **meter or safety posts** after 2031.
feel: Less trapped, though **anxious** if paid openings vanish.
S3.quote: If a robot is due for field repairs around 2034, a crew needs more than a farewell cake.
fieldNote: Karl turns the five-year warning into **measured tests** and a search for posted wages.
He hopes to create an **emergency balance**, but only from overtime left after keeping the van current.

steps.text: Try the approved diagnostic tool after crew testing
Put overtime left after van payments into emergency savings
Apply for local meter or safety-check posts after 2031
Keep paid line shifts while field repairs remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade should be used to train people properly and keep the lights on, not to sell a shiny timetable. I’d ask the company to let older junior workers demonstrate what they can do. We might still be earning at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 68 when the thinking AI arrives and 71 when the line robots do. I may have stopped climbing by then, but I do not know until we check our retirement income against the rent. This picture gives me time to pay the van off and see whether part-time inspection work is needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d sit with my partner to list our retirement income, rent and clinic wages on paper. I’d keep learning line faults from Ben and take my normal shifts. In the first year after 2036, if I’m still employed, I’d ask for fewer climbing shifts and apply for a paid ground-inspection place; if the numbers cover our bills, we could choose to stop work before the 2039 robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautiously easier about this one. I still worry about this month’s van and heating bill, so I cannot say calm. But ten years gives us a chance to decide with figures instead of a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to stop as soon as you can?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the rent is covered without relying on our daughter. I like being on the crew even as the junior man. I would rather reduce climbing than disappear from paid work too soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the company need to show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real ground-inspection post with hours and a wage, not just a course. I can learn its tools if people who do the work show me. If no such post exists, I’d stay on the line as long as I safely can.

say: I’d request **skills demonstrations** so older junior workers can show what they actually know on the job.
I’d support training tied to **real posts**.
think: The **2039 robots** may arrive after my climbing years, although I could still need paid work.
Our **retirement income** must still cover rent.
do: List **income and rent** with my partner now.
Keep **normal line shifts** while learning faults from Ben.
Apply for **paid ground inspection** after 2036 if still employed.
feel: Cautiously easier, yet **uneasy** about present bills.
S4.quote: We might still be earning at 68.
fieldNote: Karl sees the long warning as time to **check finances** and consider a lower-climbing role.
His current **van and heating bills** prevent calm, even if robots arrive after his likely field career.

steps.text: Keep normal line shifts and learn faults from Ben
Apply for paid ground-inspection work after 2036 if employed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I would be 63 when robots can take the field work, and our savings would not carry a lost wage even for a month. I need a clear list of paid roles the company expects to keep, plus time on shift to qualify for one. I’m willing to learn once I can see that the job exists.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the people still learning the trade at my age. My daughter is grown and pays her own bills, but she sometimes thinks I must have a retirement cheque waiting. I have to keep earning until the figures really add up.

headlineQuote: I have to keep earning until the figures really add up.
portrait: Karl is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** with a vocational certificate and a slower pace at fault identification.
He uses **AI tools occasionally**, yet wants proof before changing how he does a dangerous job.
His household has **less than one month** of savings, and few nearby employers offer similar work.
He hopes to reach **retirement through wages**, while checking whether any new role truly pays.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring field robots by 2031, before Karl can afford to lose his line wage.
whatWouldHelp: A list of **paid roles** and shift time to qualify for one would give Karl a usable plan.
